scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.brief: A meal-kit company runs a customer support agent on the Claude Agent SDK. Its MCP tools are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and pause_subscription. The agent may refund up to $150 per box; larger refunds go to a human.

questions.question: A hook blocks process_refund until get_customer returns a verified customer ID. It was added after refunds went to the wrong accounts. Gift boxes go to people who have no customer record, so every gift refund now goes to a human. Staff settle these quickly by matching the gift code and delivery address, and lookup_order returns both. Which change fits best?

options.t: Exempt gift boxes from the hook, and add prompt steps with examples for matching the gift code and address.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Clear steps with examples would be followed most of the time, but this check exists because refunds went to the wrong accounts, so it has to stay in code.

options.t: Keep the hook as it is, and attach a structured case summary to each gift escalation for staff.
options.why: Works, but the queue stays. A good summary helps staff work faster, but every gift refund still leaves the chat and waits for a person.

options.t: Widen the hook: a tool-confirmed match of gift code and delivery address also unlocks that refund.
options.why: Best. The gate stays in code, but it now accepts a second proof of identity that a tool confirms. Gift refunds settle in the chat without weakening the check.

options.t: Have checkout create a customer record for each gift recipient, so get_customer can verify them.
options.why: Works, but wrong home. It changes another system to fit the agent, does nothing for gifts already sent, and a record built at checkout says little about who is in the chat.

questions.decider: Staff settle these quickly by matching the gift code and delivery address, and lookup_order returns both.
questions.explanation: When a code gate blocks a legitimate path, widen what the gate accepts rather than moving the check into the prompt. Identity checks before money moves need programmatic enforcement.

eli5.question: A guard checks ID before any refund. Gift recipients have no ID card on file, so the guard sends all of them to a person. The clue: staff already check them another way, and the tools can confirm that way.
eli5.answer: Think of a door guard who only accepts one kind of pass. Some honest visitors carry a different, equally good pass. You don't fire the guard or ask visitors to vouch for themselves. You teach the guard to accept the second pass too (widen the prerequisite gate). Rule: when a code check blocks a real case, widen what the check accepts. Don't move the check into the prompt.
options: Sending the guard home and leaving a note works most days. This check exists because refunds went astray, so a note is not enough.
A tidier file for the person at the desk helps, but every gift visitor still queues at the desk.
Correct. The guard stays, and now accepts a second pass a tool can confirm.
Printing ID cards for every gift recipient changes another office, and a card made at checkout doesn't prove who is talking.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the hook is too strict, so it should step aside for gift boxes. But the hook exists because refunds went to the wrong accounts. The real gap is that it accepts only one kind of proof. A gate can accept a second proof, as long as a tool confirms it.
deep.diagram:
process_refund requested
  verified customer ID?            → allow
  gift code + address match tool?  → allow
  neither                          → block, escalate

questions.question: lookup_order can fail in two ways. Either no box matches the ID, or the order database times out. Both return isError with the text “Operation failed.” The agent sometimes tells a customer their box does not exist when the lookup only timed out. Customers often mistype box IDs. The timeouts come at evening peaks and last several minutes. Which change fits best?

options.t: Retry the database read inside lookup_order with backoff, and return the error once retries run out.
options.why: Works, but delays the problem. Retries ride out brief blips, but these timeouts last minutes, so the agent still gets the same vague error in the end.

options.t: Return an errorCategory of not_found or transient, an isRetryable flag and a short description.
options.why: Best. The agent can now tell a missing box from a timeout. It asks the customer to check a mistyped ID, and says “try again shortly” for a timeout.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each failure as “The order service is briefly unavailable.”
options.why: Works, but hides the problem. Timeout chats improve, but the hook sees the same text for a mistyped ID, so those customers are told the service is down.

options.t: Tell the agent in its prompt to ask the customer to recheck the box ID before saying it does not exist.
options.why: Works, but only usually. A recheck helps mistyped IDs, but the agent still cannot see which failure happened, so timeouts still end in a wrong answer.

questions.decider: Both return isError with the text “Operation failed.”
questions.explanation: A uniform error message stops the agent from picking the right recovery. Structured errors that separate a transient timeout from a genuine not-found let it retry or explain correctly.

eli5.question: Two very different failures come back with the same words. The agent has to guess which one happened, and sometimes guesses wrong. The clue: both return the text “Operation failed.”
eli5.answer: Picture a shop assistant who phones the stockroom. Whether the item doesn't exist or the stockroom phone is engaged, the reply is just “no”. The fix is a reply that says which kind of “no” it is (structured error with errorCategory and isRetryable). Then the assistant knows whether to say “check the code” or “try again in a minute”. Rule: different failures need different labels, so the agent can choose the right recovery.
options: Ringing again a few times helps for a quick blip. These outages last minutes, so the reply is still the same vague “no”.
Correct. The reply now says which kind of failure it was.
Saying “stockroom closed” every time is right for timeouts, but wrong for customers who mistyped their code.
Asking customers to recheck helps typos, but the assistant still can't tell when the stockroom is down.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent is careless and needs better instructions or more retries. But it is doing its best with a message that says nothing. “Operation failed” hides which failure happened, so no prompt or hook downstream can tell them apart. The tool has to say it.

questions.question: Customers can claim a refund within 30 days of delivery. The agent checks each box against that window. Delivery dates reach it in three shapes, one per warehouse system: Unix seconds, ISO dates, and a plain number such as 20260403. The agent misjudges the plain number, mostly near month ends. Another warehouse system joins soon. Which TWO changes make the answer the same for every source?

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that turns each delivery date into one ISO form before Claude reads it.
options.why: Best. Code converts every format before Claude sees it, so the plain number never reaches Claude. A new warehouse needs one more rule in the hook.

options.t: Add a convert_date tool, and tell the agent to call it before any refund-window question.
options.why: Works, but only usually. The tool converts dates correctly, but calling it is a request, so some chats will skip it.

options.t: Describe all three date shapes in the system prompt, with a worked conversion for each one.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Examples make mistakes rarer, but Claude still converts and counts the days itself, which is where the month-end errors come from.

options.t: Have lookup_order also return days_since_delivery and a within_window flag.
options.why: Best. The tool does the date maths in code, so Claude reads the answer instead of working it out, whatever the source format.

questions.decider: Delivery dates reach it in three shapes, one per warehouse system
questions.explanation: Deterministic data handling belongs in code. A hook normalises mixed formats before the model sees them, and a tool can return derived values instead of asking the model to compute them.

eli5.question: Dates arrive written three different ways, and the agent misreads one of them. Soon there will be a fourth. The clue: the answer must be the same whatever system the date came from.
eli5.answer: Imagine a post room that gets letters dated in three styles. Instead of training every clerk to read all three, you stamp one standard date on each letter as it arrives (a PostToolUse hook that normalises). Even better, the sender can write “arrived 12 days ago” on the envelope (the tool returns the computed value). Rule: format conversion and date maths belong in code, not in Claude's head.
options: Correct. Every date is stamped in one standard form before Claude reads it.
A conversion machine on the desk helps, but clerks still have to remember to use it.
A wall chart of date styles helps, but the clerk still does the sums and still slips at month ends.
Correct. The answer arrives already worked out.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think Claude needs better instructions about dates. But converting formats and counting days are exact jobs with one right answer. That is work for code. Claude should receive either one clean format or the answer already computed.

  2026-04-03  (one ISO form)
  + days_since_delivery, within_window from the tool

guide.obj: 1.5 Agent SDK hooks for interception and normalization
guide.quote: Normalize heterogeneous formats (Unix ts, ISO 8601, numeric codes)

questions.question: Many customers raise several unrelated things in one message. For example: “My salmon was spoiled, please pause next week, and where is today's box?” The agent settles the first request and ends its turn. The customer then has to write back about the rest. Each request takes one or two tool calls, and they rarely depend on each other. Which change best cuts these repeat contacts?

options.t: Spawn a subagent per request with the Task tool, and have a coordinator merge their findings into one reply.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. Subagents suit long, separate investigations. These requests take one or two tool calls each, so the coordination costs more than it saves.

options.t: End every reply by asking the customer whether anything else in their message still needs help.
options.why: Works, but leaves work undone. The question invites the customer back, but the turn still ends with requests open, so they still have to write again.

options.t: Before the loop accepts end_turn, check that the draft reply mentions each request.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Matching words catches some misses, but a reply can mention a request without settling it.

options.t: Have the agent list the separate requests first, then settle or escalate each one before it ends.
options.why: Best. A list of requests gives the agent a checklist to finish in the same contact, with no extra machinery.

questions.decider: The agent settles the first request and ends its turn.
questions.explanation: Decompose a multi-concern message into its separate requests and handle each before ending the turn. Subagents earn their overhead only when each piece needs a long, isolated investigation.

eli5.question: A customer asks three things at once, and the agent answers only the first. The clue: each request is small and they don't depend on each other.
eli5.answer: Think of a waiter given three requests at one table. A good waiter jots all three on the pad first, then brings each before walking away (decompose the request into a list and work through it). You don't need three extra waiters for three small jobs. Rule: several requests in one message → list them, then settle each before ending the turn.
options: Three extra waiters plus a head waiter works, but it's a lot of staff for three small jobs.
Asking “anything else?” is polite, but the waiter still walks away with two orders unfilled.
Checking the reply mentions each request helps, but mentioning a request is not the same as settling it.
Correct. Write the list first, then finish each item.

deep.premise: It is tempting to reach for subagents whenever a message has several parts. But subagents are for heavy, separate investigations whose output would crowd the main context. Here each request is one or two tool calls. The missing piece is simply a plan: list the requests, then finish them all.

deep.rule: Several requests in one message: list them, then settle or escalate each before ending the turn.

guide.quote: Decompose multi-concern requests; investigate in parallel with shared context

questions.question: The agent often hands customers to a person when the person then settles the case with no exception. It also handles some cases that needed an exception. In those it promises remedies the company does not offer. The escalation guidance in its system prompt is one line: “Escalate when appropriate.” An engineer proposes having Claude rate its own confidence and escalating low scores. What is the best next step?

options.t: Write clear escalate-or-resolve criteria into the prompt, with a few contrasting example cases.
options.why: Best. The agent has no real definition of when to escalate. Explicit criteria with contrasting examples fix both kinds of mistake at low cost.

options.t: Have Claude rate its confidence each turn, and escalate cases below a cut-off tuned on past chats.
options.why: Works, but weak signal. A tuned cut-off moves the balance, but Claude's own confidence does not track whether a case needs an exception, so one error trades for the other.

options.t: Train a classifier on past escalation labels to route each case before the agent replies.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A classifier is worth its cost once clear criteria are in place and still fall short. Here the guidance is one vague line, so the cheap fix comes first.

options.t: Add a sentiment check that escalates customers who sound frustrated, whatever else is going on.
options.why: Works, but wrong signal. Some upset customers do need a person, but mood does not track complexity: calm customers can need exceptions, angry ones often have simple problems.

questions.decider: The escalation guidance in its system prompt is one line: “Escalate when appropriate.”
questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence and sentiment are unreliable proxies for case complexity. When the escalation boundary is unclear, define it with explicit criteria and contrasting examples first.

eli5.question: The agent escalates the wrong cases in both directions. Someone suggests a confidence score. The clue: the only guidance it has is “Escalate when appropriate.”
eli5.answer: Imagine a new shop assistant told only “call the manager when appropriate”. Sometimes they call for nothing, sometimes they promise things they can't. Asking them how sure they feel won't help. Give them a clear list of when to call and when not to, with a few real examples (explicit criteria plus few-shot examples). Rule: unclear escalation → write the criteria first. Confidence and mood are poor signals.
options: Correct. Tell the assistant exactly when to call the manager, with examples.
Asking the assistant how sure they feel moves the line, but their feeling doesn't match which cases need the manager.
Hiring a second person to sort cases works, but costs far more than writing down the rule first. It wins only once the rule exists and still falls short.
Calling the manager for every grumpy customer misses calm customers with tricky problems.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent needs a number to decide with, like a confidence score. But the agent's own sense of confidence does not track whether a case needs a policy exception. The real gap is that nobody has told it where the line is. One vague sentence is all it has.

evidence.quote: The escalation guidance in its system prompt is one line: “Escalate when appropriate.”

deep.rule: When escalation is miscalibrated, write explicit criteria with contrasting examples first. Self-rated confidence and sentiment are poor proxies.

guide.quote: Sentiment-based escalation and self-reported confidence are unreliable proxies for complexity.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: In long chats the agent starts to slip. It rounds refund amounts and asks again for box IDs the customer already gave. Each get_customer call returns over 40 fields, and the agent calls it several times per chat. The workflow uses only a handful of those fields. The slips begin while the context window is still under half full. Which change best fixes this?

options.t: Move to a model with a larger context window, and keep the full history in every request.
options.why: Works, but delays the problem. More room helps when history gets cut off, but the window is under half full. The facts are getting buried, not dropped.

options.t: Strip each get_customer result to the values the agent needs before it joins the history.
options.why: Best. Repeated 40-field results bury the few facts that matter. Trimming them removes the noise around the amounts and IDs.

options.t: Every ten turns, summarise the older turns and replace them in the history with that summary.
options.why: Works, but loses detail. A shorter history has less noise, but summaries tend to round amounts and drop IDs, which are the very slips seen here.

options.t: Call get_customer again before each reply, so the agent works from fresh values.
options.why: Works, but adds noise. Fresh values sit near the end where Claude reads well, but each call adds another 40-field result, and it can't recover IDs the customer typed.

questions.decider: Each get_customer call returns over 40 fields, and the agent calls it several times per chat.
questions.explanation: Tool results pile up and swamp the context long before it is full. Trim verbose tool output to the fields the workflow uses, so key facts are not lost in the middle.

eli5.question: Late in long chats, the agent rounds amounts and forgets IDs. The clue: each customer lookup dumps over 40 fields, many times per chat, and the window isn't even half full.
eli5.answer: Imagine a desk where every phone call adds a 40-page printout, though you only need five lines from it. After a few calls, the important note is buried under paper. A bigger desk doesn't help. Cut each printout down to the five lines you need (trim tool results to the relevant fields). Rule: when facts get lost before the window is full, cut the noise, not the history.
options: A bigger desk holds more paper, but the note is still buried under it.
Correct. Keep only the lines you use from each printout.
Writing a short summary clears the desk, but summaries round numbers and lose IDs.
Fetching a fresh printout puts the numbers on top, but adds another 40 pages each time.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the agent is running out of room. But the window is under half full. The problem is noise: big tool results repeated many times bury the few facts that matter in the middle of the context, where models read least reliably.

evidence.means: Exact facts are being lost. Summaries ([[2]]) are known to round amounts and drop IDs.

questions.question: Over time the support agent has gained many tools. Next to the five core ones sit back-office tools such as issue_credit_memo, adjust_inventory and override_price. Each is needed in very few chats, and they are sometimes called when they should not be. Since the list grew, the agent picks the wrong core tool more often, spread across all five. Which change best reverses this?

options.t: Leave the everyday tools where they are, and move the rarely used ones to a specialist it hands off to.
options.why: Best. A short tool list on the agent that handles most chats restores reliable selection, and the rare tools stay available through the specialist.

options.t: Rewrite every tool description with inputs, examples and boundaries that set it apart from its neighbours.
options.why: Works, but a different problem. Sharper descriptions fix confusion between look-alike tools. These mistakes are spread across all the core tools and began as the list grew.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks back-office tools unless a supervisor approved the case.
options.why: Works, but a different problem. The hook stops misuse of the back-office tools, but they stay in the list, so choosing among the core tools is still harder.

options.t: Merge all the tools into a few broad ones, each taking an action parameter that names the operation.
options.why: Works, but blurs the tools. Fewer tools shortens the list, but generic action tools hide what each operation does, so selection inside them gets harder.

questions.decider: Since the list grew, the agent picks the wrong core tool more often, spread across all five.
questions.explanation: Too many tools on one agent degrades selection. Keep the high-frequency tools on the front-line agent and scope rare capabilities to a specialist.

eli5.question: The agent's toolbox got crowded, and now it grabs the wrong everyday tool more often. The clue: the mistakes spread across all five core tools and began as the list grew.
eli5.answer: Think of a kitchen drawer stuffed with gadgets you use once a year. Finding the everyday knife gets slower and sloppier. You move the rare gadgets to a cupboard in the back room (a specialist agent) and keep the drawer for daily tools. Rule: too many tools → keep the frequent ones on the main agent, move rare ones to a specialist.
options: Correct. Clear the drawer; rare gadgets live with a specialist.
Better labels help when two tools look alike. Here the drawer is simply too full.
Locking the rare gadgets stops misuse, but they still clutter the drawer.
Gluing gadgets into a few multi-tools empties the drawer, but now each tool is harder to tell apart inside.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think wrong tool picks always mean bad descriptions. That is true when two tools look alike. But when errors are spread across every tool and started as the list grew, the cause is the number of tools. Selection gets less reliable as one agent holds more of them.

questions.question: The description of escalate_to_human is one line. It reads: “Escalate the conversation to a human manager or supervisor.” The agent calls it when customers say things like “my office manager ordered this box”. Most needless handoffs come from messages like that. The same tool also handles refunds above the agent's limit. The other tools have full descriptions with inputs and boundaries. What is the most effective first step?

options.t: Add example chats to the system prompt where a customer mentions a manager and the agent carries on.
options.why: Works, but works around the cause. Examples help once the description is clear. Here the one-line description is what invites the mistake, so fix it first.

options.t: Add a line to the system prompt saying a mention of a manager is not a request for a person.
options.why: Works, but wrong home. The prompt line patches one wording. The tool description is where Claude decides which tool to call, and it still says “manager”.

options.t: Split the tool into request_person and escalate_large_refund, each with its own inputs.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt for a first step. Purpose-specific tools can be good design, but it is more work, and each new tool still needs a proper description.

options.t: Rewrite the description: when to hand over, when not to, and what the handoff needs as input.
options.why: Best. Descriptions are the main signal for choosing a tool. Stating the real triggers and exclusions fixes the keyword match where it starts.

questions.decider: It reads: “Escalate the conversation to a human manager or supervisor.”
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection. When a description is minimal, expanding it with when to use it, when not to, and its inputs is the highest-leverage first step.

eli5.question: The agent hands people over whenever they mention a manager, even in passing. The clue: the tool's description is one line that literally says “manager”.
eli5.answer: Think of a door labelled only “Manager”. People walk through it whenever the word comes up. Rewrite the sign to say who should use the door, who shouldn't, and what to bring (a full tool description). The sign is where the choice is made. Rule: a minimal tool description is the first thing to fix when Claude picks a tool wrongly.
options: Showing examples helps once the sign is clear. Today the sign itself causes the mistake.
A note elsewhere about the word “manager” patches one case, but the door still says “Manager”.

questions.question: The loop checks stop_reason. On tool_use, it runs the tool and sends the output back as a new user message, rewritten as a plain sentence. The assistant turn that asked for the tool is not added to the history. The agent sometimes looks up a box it has just looked up. Once it told a customer a refund went through when none was made. Which change fixes this?

options.t: Send each tool result back as its raw structured output instead of a rewritten sentence.
options.why: Works, but a different problem. Raw output keeps fields that rewording can drop, but Claude still has no record of which calls it made.

options.t: Keep a case-facts block listing each tool call made so far and its result in every request.
options.why: Works, but works around the cause. It rebuilds the call record by hand, while the loop keeps dropping the real one.

options.t: Keep each tool_use request from Claude in the history, followed by its tool_result.
options.why: Best. Each call and its result sit in the history as a pair, so Claude can see what it already did and what came back.

options.t: Add a hook that blocks a second lookup_order call for a box already looked up.
options.why: Works, but treats one symptom. It stops repeat lookups, but Claude can still claim a refund it never requested.

questions.decider: The assistant turn that asked for the tool is not added to the history.
questions.explanation: In the agentic loop, the assistant's tool_use turn and the matching tool_result must both be appended to the history. Dropping either leaves Claude without a record of what it did.

eli5.question: The agent repeats lookups it just did and claims actions it never took. The clue: the turn where Claude asked for the tool is never saved.
eli5.answer: Imagine a diary where you write down the answers you got, but never the questions you asked. Later you can't tell what you already asked, or whether you actually did something. The fix is to write both lines every time: the request and its answer (tool_use and tool_result as a pair in the history). Rule: every tool call goes into the history with its result.
options: Copying answers word for word is tidier, but the questions are still missing from the diary.
Keeping a separate notes page works, but it rebuilds by hand what the diary should already hold.
Correct. Write the request and its answer, every time.
Blocking repeat lookups stops one symptom, but the agent can still claim a refund it never asked for.

deep.premise: It is tempting to blame the rewritten sentences, since rewording can lose details. But losing a field does not explain repeating a lookup that just ran, or claiming a refund that was never called. Those need a missing record of the calls. The loop drops the assistant turn that holds each tool_use.

questions.question: When the agent escalates, it attaches the full chat transcript. Staff say picking up a handoff now takes longer than handling the case from scratch. Most of that time goes on working out what the agent already tried and why it stopped. Usually the person only has to approve or decline one refund. Which handoff design serves staff best?

options.t: Attach only the last five turns of the chat, where the reason to escalate usually shows up.
options.why: Works, but loses history. Fewer turns are quicker to read, but the earlier steps are exactly what staff are trying to work out.

options.t: Send a structured summary: IDs, root cause, steps tried, the amount and a recommended action.
options.why: Best. Staff see what was tried, why it stopped and what is proposed in one place, so approving or declining is quick.

options.t: Pin the customer ID, box ID and refund amount in a header above the unchanged transcript.
options.why: Works, but a different problem. The header speeds up finding IDs, but staff still read the whole chat to learn what was tried and why it stopped.

options.t: Replace the transcript with one reason code from a fixed list of escalation categories.
options.why: Works, but too thin. A code helps route the case, but it loses the amount, the cause and what was already tried.

questions.decider: Most of that time goes on working out what the agent already tried and why it stopped.
questions.explanation: A person picking up an escalation needs a structured handoff: identifiers, root cause, what was tried, the amount and a recommended action. They should not have to read the transcript to get it.

eli5.question: Staff get the whole chat and spend ages working out what happened. The clue: the slow part is learning what the agent tried and why it stopped.
eli5.answer: Think of a nurse handing over at shift change. They don't hand over a recording of the whole day. They give a short sheet: who, what's wrong, what was tried, what's pending, what they suggest (a structured handoff summary). Rule: hand a person a summary with IDs, root cause, steps tried, amount and recommended action.
options: The last few minutes of the recording are shorter, but the earlier steps are what the next nurse needs.
Correct. A short handover sheet with everything needed to decide.
A name tag on the recording helps find the patient, but you still have to play the whole recording.
A one-word code helps send the patient to the right ward, but says nothing about what was tried.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the human just needs the key IDs pulled out. But finding IDs is not the slow part. The time goes on rebuilding what the agent tried and why it stopped. A structured summary answers that directly, so the person can decide without reading the chat.
